findings.reason: the plan's host allow-list is the mechanism the read depends on, and either §2's rule and done-when must be widened to name the production host or §4 is unbuildable; the conflicting arms cannot be satisfied at once.
findings.text: §4 reads the file "from the production instance", but §2 (plan.html:46-47, `done`) states "Requests go only to the integration instance" and its done-when refuses "a request to any host other than the integration instance and the listed sign-in hosts"; §4's own done-when then asks that "every write-refusal and host-refusal test of section 2 holds for the production host", which, as §2 is written, refuses the very host §4 must read, so the two arms cannot both pass

findings.reason: a section declared `implementable` on an endpoint its own evidence does not show to exist sends the worker at a GET file read that may not be offered, and the only visible fallbacks are the non-GET service call and the legacy host the guardrails refuse, so the node stalls or reaches the forbidden path.
findings.text: §4 asserts a file served by production under GET/HEAD as an established endpoint, while the decision behind it records "No file was fetched and no other host was contacted", and §1 (plan.html:40) records that for IDM downloads "the plan's only leads are a legacy service call returning a document's current version and a legacy download path", so no evidence in the plan shows a production GET operation returns file bytes

findings.reason: the arm cannot fail on the most likely wrong outcome of the read this section delivers; it needs a stated check on the stored bytes (the spreadsheet arm already has one through sheet names and row counts).
findings.text: the PDF half of §4's done-when records only that a body of some size and digest was stored, with no check that the bytes are the document, so a 401 page or an HTML login redirect — the failure the decision context itself records — passes the arm unchanged
